intro: Un bal, the second movement of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14, is a waltz marked Allegro non troppo, with two harps playing above the strings. The beloved’s melody enters within the waltz, drops out and later returns once more.

sections.label: Intro · Strings in tremolo, two harps
sections.mNote: Rising harp figures lead towards the dance.

sections.label: A · Waltz theme, violins, A major
sections.mNote: A major waltz tune in the violins over pizzicato bass.

sections.label: B · Idée fixe in waltz time
sections.mNote: Flute and oboe play the idée fixe in waltz rhythm.

sections.label: A′ · Waltz theme returns in A
sections.mNote: Strings and winds take up the waltz again.

sections.label: B′ · Clarinet solo, idée fixe
sections.mNote: The strings stop for a short clarinet solo.

sections.label: Coda · Tempo primo, con fuoco
sections.mNote: The waltz accelerates to its close.

cues.title: Introduction, harps and tremolo strings
cues.text: The strings play a tremolo while two harp parts enter in turn with rising broken chords. The sound grows louder. Then the first violins begin the waltz.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 1–38, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 1–4: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Waltz theme, first violins
cues.text: The waltz opens softly in A major. First violins play the tune, while cellos and double basses pluck the first beat of each bar. The melody rises and turns above this pizzicato bass.
cues.evidence: Movement II, waltz from bar 38, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 4–5: violin melody and pizzicato bass accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Programme of the second movement
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme places the artist at a brilliant party, where he sees his beloved, as he also sees her in the countryside. The ballroom has its own music. With her comes the melody heard since the start of the symphony.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, programme of Symphonie fantastique, part II, in the 1845 and 1855 versions: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Idée fixe in waltz time
cues.text: Flute and oboe play the beloved’s melody, now recast in three beats to the bar. Beneath it the strings keep the waltz going, with soft chords above running figures in the cellos and basses. A clarinet then takes up the theme.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 120–162; flute and oboe begin the idée fixe, followed by clarinet. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 11–14.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Revision in Florence, April 1831
cues.text: In Florence in April 1831, Berlioz reorchestrated the movement and wrote a new coda. The waltz had already pleased the audience at the Paris première.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 34, and the composition history at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm : Florence, April 1831, reorchestration and new coda.

cues.title: Return of the waltz, A major
cues.text: The waltz returns in A major, after the central idée fixe. Its tune passes between strings and woodwinds, and the harps add rippling figures and chords.
cues.evidence: Movement II, returning waltz following the central idée fixe, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 15–23.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Idée fixe, solo clarinet
cues.text: The strings stop. A solo clarinet begins the idée fixe again, accompanied by a brief flute phrase, quiet horns and harp chords. After a few bars the dance returns and the melody breaks off.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 302–319, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 31–32; the string parts rest through the exposed continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, from bar 320
cues.text: Tempo primo con fuoco, the first tempo, with fire. The strings return at speed and the woodwinds join them, with chords from both harp parts. The dance ends emphatically in A major.
cues.evidence: Movement II, coda from bar 320, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 33–37: tempo marking, orchestration and A-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violins begin the waltz
transitions.from: Intro · Strings in tremolo, two harps
transitions.to: A · Waltz theme, violins, A major
transitions.how: The rising harps and tremolo strings stop. First violins begin the waltz softly in A major, with cellos and basses playing pizzicato on the first beat. Second violins and violas play the lighter chords between those bass notes.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 32–49; Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 4.

transitions.title: Idée fixe enters in the waltz
transitions.from: A · Waltz theme, violins, A major
transitions.to: B · Idée fixe in waltz time
transitions.how: The A major waltz thins out to soft string chords. Flute and oboe begin the idée fixe in the same triple metre. Cellos and basses add running figures below it, and the clarinet takes over the melody as the phrase continues.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 111–137; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 11–12.

transitions.title: Return of the waltz in A major
transitions.from: B · Idée fixe in waltz time
transitions.to: A′ · Waltz theme returns in A
transitions.how: In bars 156–192, at the end of the central idée fixe section, the wind melody finishes and the strings play a rising line. The waltz returns in A major. Plucked bass notes mark the first beat, bowed strings play the quick figures, and winds and horns play above them. The triple metre continues unchanged.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, end of the central idée fixe and return, bars 156–192; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 14–17.

transitions.title: Solo clarinet recalls the idée fixe
transitions.from: A′ · Waltz theme returns in A
transitions.how: The waltz slows and the strings stop. A solo clarinet recalls the idée fixe over quiet horns and harp chords, and the flute adds a short phrase. The string bass has dropped out, and with it the regular tread of the dance.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 298–319; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 31–32.

transitions.title: Return of the strings at Tempo primo
transitions.how: The clarinet’s recollection ends. At Tempo primo con fuoco the strings return in A major with quick rising figures, and the wind and both harp parts join them. Bass notes and repeated chords carry the last bars to the close.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 320–368; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 33–37.

source.title: Berlioz, Un bal — orchestral score without the optional cornet
source.locator: Introduction and waltz, bars 1–119; central idée fixe, bars 120–162; short return, bars 302–319; coda from bar 320.

timeline.note: Tremolo strings prepare the successive entries of the two harp parts.
First violins play the waltz over bowed inner strings and plucked bass notes.
Woodwinds and strings exchange the dance tune; harps add chords and rising figures.
Flute and oboe introduce the idée fixe above soft string chords; clarinet joins them.
The returning waltz spreads from strings to woodwinds, horns and harps.
A solo clarinet recalls the beloved, with brief flute, horn and harp phrases. The strings rest.
Strings, winds and both harp parts play the final dance in A major.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and said that he was tired, so the boy did not have to explain his tears. Berlioz recorded the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt the flute and guitar, studied maps of distant islands and was deeply moved by the story of Virgil’s abandoned queen.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
